slides.title: Factorization Lemma: Local Loops from a Null-Homotopy
slides.notes: Open by naming the purpose of the appendix: it is not a new geometric object, but a conversion tool. The theorem takes a contraction of one loop and turns it into finitely many local loops, so later bundle and holonomy arguments can work with data that lives inside controlled neighborhoods.

slides.title: Why a Global Homotopy Is Too Coarse
slides.notes: Emphasize the mismatch of scale. A homotopy proves that the loop dies globally, but most differential-geometric constructions are patched together locally. The factorization lemma bridges that mismatch by replacing the global square with a finite inventory of patch-sized loops and harmless backtracking pieces.

slides.title: Curves Are Compared with Endpoints Held Fixed
slides.notes: Set up the square carefully because the rest of the proof reads its boundary. The vertical sides are not decorative; they keep the endpoints locked. That lock is what allows the boundary pieces to be inserted, canceled, and multiplied without changing the based homotopy class being analyzed.

slides.title: Continuous Homotopy Can Be Made Piecewise Ck
slides.notes: Present this as the technical cleaning step before the main factorization. The proof does not magically smooth a wild global object all at once. It refines the square until every small rectangle is chart-controlled, then performs local replacements that preserve the boundary information needed for the next argument.

slides.title: The Covering Chooses the Resolution
slides.notes: Stress that the open cover is not chosen for convenience after the proof. It is part of the input. If the later argument needs bundle charts, normal neighborhoods, or domains of a local equivalence, the subdivision adapts the homotopy square to exactly that prescribed local scale.

slides.title: A U-Lasso Is a Conjugated Local Loop
slides.notes: Use the lasso picture to separate two roles. The small loop alpha is where the local geometric calculation happens. The path mu is bookkeeping: it moves the loop to the chosen base point and moves back again, making it possible to multiply many local contributions as based loops.

slides.title: Backtracking Pieces Carry No Net Curve
slides.notes: Pause here because students often confuse the equivalence relation with ordinary equality of paths. The proof is algebraic about words in path segments. Opposite traversals of the same small edge appear constantly, and the equivalence relation gives permission to erase those adjacent out-and-back factors.

slides.title: Statement in Working Form
slides.notes: Give the theorem in the form an instructor will actually use. The conclusion is not merely that the curve is trivial. It says the triviality can be witnessed by finitely many local loop terms, each transported to the base point and each compatible with the prescribed open covering.

slides.title: Divide the Homotopy Square into Small Cells
slides.notes: The grid is the heart of the proof, so linger on it. The homotopy square is compact and the cover is open, so a sufficiently fine mesh has images small enough for local control. The finite number of cells is exactly why the final factorization contains a finite word.

slides.title: One Cell Produces One Local Lasso
slides.notes: Describe the lasso before naming formulas. In the parameter square, the path walks from the origin to a selected grid cell, goes around that cell, and returns. Applying the homotopy sends the small cell boundary into one open set, producing exactly the conjugated local loop needed in the theorem.

slides.title: Product Order Makes Interior Edges Cancel
slides.notes: Make the algebraic nature explicit. Each cell lasso contributes a small boundary word plus a corridor to the base point. The chosen product order aligns shared edges with the reverse orientation supplied by neighboring cells, so repeated backtrack cancellations leave only the outer boundary of the homotopy square.

slides.title: Piecewise Ck Boundaries Give Smooth Local Loops
slides.notes: Connect the technical lemma with the main theorem. Once the homotopy has been made piecewise Ck, choosing a finer mesh ensures every cell lies in a smooth patch of the homotopy. The lasso loop around the cell then has the smoothness required for differential-geometric operations.

slides.title: Local Lassos Feed Bundle and Holonomy Arguments
slides.notes: Relate the appendix back to the course. In bundle arguments, calculations often require a single trivialization or a single coordinate neighborhood. The lemma says a globally null loop can be tested through a finite set of such local pieces, making it a quiet but powerful support result.

slides.title: Failure Modes to Watch
slides.notes: Use these as a diagnostic checklist while students reconstruct the proof. The lasso terminology can hide three requirements: the cells must be small enough, the loop must return to the chosen base point, and the algebra must permit deletion of immediate reverse traversals.

slides.title: A 2 by 2 Grid Shows the Mechanism
slides.notes: Run this as a board exercise. With only four cells, everyone can see the path word and the reverse edge cancellations. After that concrete case, the m by m proof feels like iteration of the same local move rather than a mysterious indexing formula.

slides.title: Instructor Lab: Rebuild the Factorization
slides.notes: This exercise turns the proof into an inspection task. A good answer should not simply trace a path. It should identify the local cell loop, the conjugating corridor to the base point, and at least one future cancellation with a neighboring lasso in the product.

slides.title: The Factorization Machine
slides.notes: Close by presenting the lemma as a reusable machine. Feed in a null-homotopic based curve, choose the open cover demanded by the geometry, refine the homotopy square, and read off a finite lasso word. That machine is what later local-to-global bundle arguments quietly need.
